opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, it comes down to timing and conditions lining up in a way that doesn't happen very often.

I've spent most of my career on generative models, first images, then video, then 3D and world modeling. For a long time, the question in the back of my mind was: what is all of this ultimately for? Generating a beautiful picture is impressive, but I always felt the deeper goal was to build systems that actually understand the physical world: how objects move, how they interact, what happens when you push something. That understanding matters most when an intelligent agent has to act in the real world. So embodied intelligence felt like the natural place where the work I'd been doing could really pay off.

Ant Lingbo gave me the chance to work on that directly. A few things made it feel like a real opportunity rather than just another project.

First, the problem is still wide open. In language, the paradigm is relatively clear now. In embodied AI, we're still figuring out the basics: what the right data is, what the right model architecture is, how you get generalization rather than a robot that only works in one lab. When the foundations aren't settled, there's room to make contributions that change the direction of the field.

Second, doing this seriously requires sustained, long-term commitment: compute, data infrastructure, hardware collaboration, and the patience to not chase a demo every three months. Having an organization willing to invest on that horizon matters a lot. Many good ideas die because nobody gives them enough time.

Third, the team. You can't do something substantial alone. What excites me is being able to bring together people who care about the fundamental problems, people from vision, graphics, robotics, and learning, and let them work closely on one shared goal.

So when I say "substantial," I don't mean big in a flashy sense. I mean something that, looking back in five or ten years, actually moved the field forward, where we could say our work helped machines understand and interact with the world in a meaningful way. That's the kind of thing I want to spend these years on.

r002.rationale: It presents Ant Lingbo as a chance to advance generative and embodied AI while building systems that understand and act in the physical world.

r003.rationale: It says embodied AI’s foundations are unsettled and contributions could change the field’s direction, but does not state that this creates room to contribute to the robotics industry.

r004.rationale: The response does not say that exploring an ultimately incorrect technological path can itself benefit the robotics industry.

fable-5.1.text:
When I joined, honestly the first thing that struck me wasn't the resources or the brand, it was that the problem itself was still open. A lot of people assume that by now the path for large models is fixed, that you just follow what the leading labs have done and scale. But if you look carefully at the kind of model we actually want, something that can perceive the world, understand it, and generate it in a unified way, nobody has really solved that yet. The gap between where we are and where that vision sits is big enough that there's genuine room to contribute, not just to replicate.

The second thing is the environment. At Ant, the team is young and the organization has been willing to let us take a longer view. We're not asked to ship a demo every quarter to justify ourselves. That matters a lot in research, because the ideas that end up mattering usually look unproductive for the first year or two. I've been in places where the pressure to show results quickly ends up quietly killing the directions that would have been most interesting. Here I feel we have a window to actually test some ideas properly.

And then there's the connection to real scenarios. Ant has payments, finance, services that touch hundreds of millions of people. When you train a model, data and deployment feedback are as important as the architecture, and having access to real problems grounds the research in a way that pure academic work sometimes doesn't. So when I say "do something substantial," I mean the combination: an unsolved problem, patience from the organization, and a real-world loop to close. You don't often get all three at once, and when you do, it feels like you have an obligation to try something ambitious rather than something safe.

astra-6.text: For me, it’s the chance to take an idea beyond a demonstration and turn it into something people actually use. There’s a big difference between showing that a technology can work and making it useful and reliable in everyday situations. I see Ant Lingbo as an opportunity to work on that gap. If we can solve a real problem and keep improving the solution, then we’re building something with lasting value. That’s what makes the opportunity substantial to me.

That’s the opportunity I see at Ant Lingbo—and why I want to put my energy into it.
